title: How To Scope A Complex UX Engagement
excerpt: Scoping a complex UX engagement does not require a complete specification from the client. Creative Navy scopes from direct exposure to the product, operational questions, and a Creative Navy-written scope with a sprint-level cost cap.

bodyMarkdown:
## Creative Navy scope definition for complex UX engagements

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Scoping a complex UX engagement is more straightforward for the client than many organisations expect. Creative Navy does not require a complete specification, a complete feature inventory, or a fully resolved problem statement before scope can be defined.

Creative Navy needs access to the product itself and a conversation about what the client believes is wrong. Product access can be a walkthrough, a demo environment, or screenshots. The scope document, cost estimate, and phasing are Creative Navy's output, not the client's preparation.

The scoping walkthrough takes 30 to 60 minutes. It does not cost the client anything. It is part of how Creative Navy determines whether and how to engage, not a billable phase.

## Inputs Creative Navy needs before writing a scope

Creative Navy scopes a UX engagement from direct exposure to the system rather than from description alone. Description of a complex software product is usually incomplete, and the gap between the description and the operating reality often contains the most important scoping decisions.

For an existing product, the existing interface is the primary evidence base. Its structure shows accumulated design decisions, visible workarounds, places where users need explanation, and gaps between what the interface communicates and what the product actually does.

For a new product, Creative Navy examines what is known about the domain, the user, and the intended operation. The amount that remains undetermined affects how much exploratory work the Sandbox Experiments phase will need before design decisions can be grounded.

Creative Navy also asks about technical architecture, regulatory requirements, timeline, team structure, and budget. These constraints shape what an engagement can produce. In Creative Navy's scoping model, constraints are design parameters rather than obstacles.

## What Creative Navy assesses during the scoping walkthrough

Creative Navy uses the walkthrough to understand the product at an operational level. The question is what the system does, for whom, under which conditions, and through which primary workflows and user roles.

Creative Navy also assesses what exists and what does not yet exist. In a production system, existing screens and workflows show where design decisions have accumulated. In a new product, unresolved domain knowledge, user knowledge, or operational assumptions determine how much domain learning is required before design work can begin.

Creative Navy asks operational questions that are harder to answer than feature-list questions. Examples include what happens in abnormal system states, how the workflow behaves under peak conditions, what consequences follow from specific user errors, and what has already been tried.

These questions affect scope because different operational problems require different engagement shapes. A system whose problems appear mainly under abnormal conditions is scoped differently from a system whose problems sit in routine workflows. A product with three user roles and incompatible information needs is scoped differently from a product with one user type.

## Creative Navy writes the scope document

Creative Navy writes the scope document for the engagement. A client specification or brief can be useful input, but the engagement scope is not a client document for Creative Navy to review and price.

The scope of a UX engagement for a complex product is not a feature list or a functional specification. It is a description of the design problem and the method that will address it, structured so that the cost estimate is auditable.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

A Creative Navy scope document includes four parts: Creative Navy's description of the problem as understood from the walkthrough and initial conversation; the phases of Critical Systems Design that the engagement will work through; a sprint-level breakdown of the work; and a cost estimate that functions as a budget cap.

One-week sprints are the fixed cadence used across Creative Navy engagements. The sprint cadence does not vary by engagement size, domain, or phase. It is the rhythm at which work is produced and reviewed, and it is the unit used to construct the cost estimate.

## How the cost estimate works as a budget cap

Creative Navy's cost estimate at scoping functions as a budget cap. The engagement is not open-ended. The scope defines what will be addressed, and the estimate defines what it will cost.

If the work takes fewer sprints than estimated, the cost is lower. The cost does not exceed the estimate without a formal change to scope.

This is not fixed-price in the sense of a fixed deliverable at a fixed cost regardless of what emerges. In complex systems work, user research findings, technical constraints, or operational conditions can show that the design problem is larger or different from what the initial walkthrough suggested.

When that happens, Creative Navy raises the finding, describes what it means for scope, and agrees with the client whether to address it within the existing scope or extend it. The estimate does not silently expand.

The client enters the engagement with a defined scope and a clear cost ceiling. The remaining uncertainty sits in the design problem: what Sandbox Experiments will find, what Concept Convergence will explore, and how the evidence will develop.

## What scoping does not require from the client

Creative Navy does not require a formal specification before scoping a complex UX engagement. Creative Navy has scoped engagements with no client documentation and with documentation that described a different product from the one that emerged in conversation. A specification can provide context, but it is not the basis for scope.

Creative Navy does not require agreement on the design solution before scoping. The scoping document defines the design problem and the method. It does not define the solution, because the solution is what the engagement produces.

Creative Navy does not require a fully formed brief. The scoping conversation starts from the client's current state of clarity. This connects to Creative Navy's guidance on briefing a project when the problem is still fuzzy.

## Scope patterns for different engagement types

Creative Navy uses the same scoping process across engagement types, but the walkthrough focuses on different evidence depending on the product state and the binding constraint.

### Existing products with known problems

For an existing product with known problems, Creative Navy focuses the walkthrough on the live system and the known failure modes. Scope is usually built around the Critical Systems Design phases required to address them: Sandbox Experiments to characterise the problems at enough specificity, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, and Organizational Integration. Implementation Partnership scope depends on what the client team needs to maintain and extend the system independently.

### Existing products with undefined problems

For an existing product with observable but undefined problems, Creative Navy scopes a stronger Sandbox Experiments phase. That can mean more research depth, more competitive analysis, and broader user research before design decisions can be grounded.

The IDEXX Animana engagement is the stated exemplar in this category. Creative Navy carried out a 35-clinic, 150-plus participant research programme before design work began, because the brief was deliberately non-prescriptive and the problem needed characterisation before it could be addressed.

### New products

For a new product, Creative Navy scopes around the domain, the user, and the intended operation rather than around an existing interface. The depth of the unknown determines how much domain learning is required before design can begin.

The Greenlight engagement and the Owkin / K engagement illustrate different new-product scoping conditions. Greenlight was a safety incident reporting system built from a doctoral thesis, so Creative Navy's scoping had to account for extracting implicit knowledge from a founder's research. Owkin / K was a biomedical AI tool for clinicians in a field Creative Navy was entering from outside, so Creative Navy's scoping had to account for learning enough of an operational domain to design for its practitioners.

### New products bound by an external deadline

For a new product bound by an immovable external deadline, Creative Navy scopes by triage against the deadline. The question becomes what must appear in the demo, what is built only if time allows, and what is sacrificable.

The IMServ engagement is the stated exemplar. An energy data services company needed a clickable pitch prototype to win a competitive tender, scoped to a single one-week build sprint against the tender demo date. The artefact was deliberately disposable, and the convergence phase was compressed so the information hierarchy, UI direction, and screen set were committed quickly.

The IMServ case also shows that a compressed front end does not necessarily mean a truncated engagement. After the tender was won, the one-week prototype was followed by a multi-month Implementation Partnership supporting the client's newly created internal design team toward independent operation. The tender win and partnership to independence are client-reported; there are no measured user outcomes because the artefact was a buyer-facing pitch prototype.

## Documented engagement structures show how scope decisions differ

Documented Creative Navy engagements show that scoping discipline is not the same as choosing the largest possible engagement. The common feature is that scope decisions are made in advance and in the open.

Streetec GmbH commissioned a small, bounded engagement for kntrl 2 that shipped. The scope was six one-week sprints: three UX sprints followed by three UI sprints. Implementation support was limited to a kickoff session with Streetec's engineers and one further session four weeks into development.

AIT commissioned a fixed-scope engagement for a heat-pump controller. The scope was eight one-week sprints with discovery and requirements inside the block: five UX sprints followed by three UI sprints, with the third UI sprint used for brand theming. Creative Navy delivered 29 screens and a clickable prototype deliberately scoped to the scenario-editing flow. Implementation Partnership lasted five months and consisted of three scheduled progress meetings and eight support tickets answered.

The MDU, a ship motion monitoring system, was scoped as five sprints: two UX sprints followed by three UI sprints. Creative Navy delivered 18 screens across 45 versions, a clickable prototype, and a formal handover of the design. Creative Navy also briefed each third-party development agency the manufacturer was considering so that each could pitch on a common understanding of the delivered design. Implementation support was provided, but its duration and substance are not recorded.

Assemblio GmbH commissioned a nine one-week sprint engagement for the Assemblio Composer and the Assemblio Smart Viewer. The engagement delivered 87 screens in 233 variants, with variants covering states such as hover, selected, empty, loading, expanded, collapsed, and error. Creative Navy recorded five rounds of written feedback in which the client received named alternatives and gave reasons for choices.

Egma commissioned twelve sprints for Egma Order, structured as a UX phase producing wireframes followed by a UI phase producing the interface and design system. Scope covered the web platform, a native mobile application, and the administration area across four order types. When remaining time looked short during the UI phase, Creative Navy stated the prioritisation openly rather than silently descoping.

Topera shows a scope decision with a stated price. Creative Navy scoped a full design of the platform at twenty-four one-week sprints and put that position to the client before the engagement began. The client commissioned three one-week sprints as a concept design. The three-sprint scope produced 24 unique screens, four complete UI style directions for the same screen, a style guide, a Work Breakdown Structure view designed from two entry points, and designs for states as well as screens. It did not include user research, usability testing, a record of client decisions between alternatives, a build, an implemented component, or a development handover.

In a European industrial automation engagement, Creative Navy began with a separately scoped expert review, then six one-week sprints of design, then an ongoing retainer at two weeks per month for twelve months. In a second workstream for a touchscreen control product, Creative Navy put one, two, and three sprint options to the client and argued in writing that a single sprint would create structurally incomplete foundations with hidden downstream cost. The client chose the three-sprint option.

KISPE Space shows a consultative exploration ending at a decision gate. The exploration phase of the project was explicitly consultative, and detailed UX and UI scope was confirmed at its conclusion. The exploration phase ended at a board review where Creative Navy put twelve working decisions and a recommended development sequence to KISPE's board. The board endorsed the architecture as the working direction, approved a staged scope with explicit decision gates for uncertain features, and authorised the seven-sprint UX development phase. This was a commissioning decision, not user validation and not an outcome.

Schone Airspace Group shows a separate consultative exploration. The client commissioned the redesign of a ground control station interface for connected aircraft, and the exploration phase of the project was scope-setting. The four exploration sprints converted into a twelve-sprint programme, which converted into a twelve-month retainer at biweekly involvement.

Raymarine shows rescoping as reallocation rather than a change order. Scope was rebalanced inside the phase: plot variations were reduced to viable core alternatives, the cross-screen control contract was established before screens were detailed, critical flows were reworked against one consistent input model, and hardware and firmware dependencies were identified before handover. The two-week exploration and the eight-week programme were unchanged, with no additional sprint and no change to the fee assumption.

The maritime VTS engagement shows what it looks like when Creative Navy recommends less work than the brief asked for. Discovery replaced a common modern interface across nine products with one application developed to full depth as a reference, a technology-neutral semantic design system, bounded transfer tests in four other products, and implementation contracts and governance for the client's engineers. The reference product was selected with a weighted scorecard agreed in advance: commercial significance 25%, system transfer value 25%, access to representative users 20%, high-consequence UX learning 15%, and implementation feasibility 15%. Five candidates were scored out of 100: VTS 90, inland vessel tracking 77, voice communications 71, electronic reporting 67, and lock planning 63.

The handheld C2 engagement shows scope stated as a constraint before work began. The engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and clarity of operator control. It did not cover autonomy, control algorithms, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification, or weapons-review activity. The delivery plan stated that the scale of the system exceeded the size of the project, and four areas were selected as a consequence. Every sprint ended with Creative Navy flagging opportunities to pursue and opportunities to ignore, with the decision resting with the client.

Oceaneering shows a contingency named in advance and spent where the work proved hardest. The phase structure was a discovery sprint, then four one-week UX sprints including a contingency sprint, then three and a half UI sprints. Creative Navy delivered 54 screens, with 321 screens counted with variations. The contingency sprint was spent on UX because the UX work proved to be the most complex part of the engagement.

## Evidence boundaries for scoping examples

The documented engagement structures above are evidence of how scope was constructed and managed. They are not, by themselves, measured outcomes.

Sprint counts, screen counts, team sizes, support ticket counts, feedback rounds, and version counts describe the work performed. They should not be read as proof of product effect unless a separate measured or reported outcome is stated.

Topera is a concept design only. Nothing in the Topera scope should be read as a built product, deployment, pilot, or user outcome. The twenty-four-sprint figure is Creative Navy's professional estimate of the full scope, not a measured comparison between two pieces of work.

The IMServ outcome described here is client-reported. The tender was won and a later partnership followed, but there are no measured user outcomes because the artefact was a buyer-facing pitch prototype.

## Related buying guidance

Creative Navy's guidance on briefing a project when the problem is still fuzzy explains why a complete brief is not required before scoping begins.

Creative Navy's guidance on buying design work for regulated or critical systems is relevant where technical architecture, regulatory requirements, operational risk, or implementation responsibility shape the scope.

Creative Navy's guidance on evaluating a UX partner for complex products is relevant when comparing how prospective partners ask operational questions, price uncertainty, and make scope decisions visible before work begins.
